title_de: Pay-Day für Purdy – Warum sich die 49ers und ihre Fans nicht vor einem neuen Vertrag fürchten müssen
teaser_de: Warum sich die 49ers und ihre Fans vor einem neuen Vertrag für Brock Purdy nicht fürchten müssen.
title_en: Payday for Purdy: why the 49ers and their fans need not fear a new contract
teaser_en: Why the 49ers and their fans need not fear a new contract for Brock Purdy.
body_en:
![Payday for Purdy](https://i0.wp.com/theninerempiregermany.de/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/payday.png?fit=1024%2C768&ssl=1)

With the final whistle of the last game of the 2024 regular season against the Arizona Cardinals on January 5, 2025, a pivotal opportunity opens up for the San Francisco 49ers: they are finally allowed to negotiate their shared future with quarterback Brock Purdy and his agent Kyle Strongin. From that point on, Purdy, whose third year on his rookie contract will then be complete, is eligible under the CBA (the collective bargaining agreement between the NFL and the NFLPA) to begin talks about a contract extension. But since the end of last season, a number of questions have sparked extensive debate, not only among the Faithful but across the entire NFL bubble: What contract will Purdy get? How many millions will he earn? Will the 49ers still be a contender with an expensive QB contract, or will they slide into mediocrity, which, given the season that is just ending, is unfortunately not an unfounded fear?

This article therefore aims to shed some light on the matter. It explains what really matters when assessing contracts in the NFL and what is merely media-friendly PR by the agent. It also uses several examples to show how other teams have handled such a situation (and stayed successful afterwards) and what different scenarios for Purdy and the 49ers could look like.

### How to properly evaluate and analyze quarterback contracts in the NFL

Quarterback contracts are the financial backbone of an NFL team. Structuring these contracts the right way determines not only a team's sporting future but also its economic stability. While many media outlets and fans tend to focus on figures such as "average per year" (APY) or "average annual value" (AAV), these values are misleading because they take into account neither a team's actual financial obligations nor the strategic options in contract management. In fact, these figures are usually pure advertising messages from agents who want to showcase their negotiating skills to become more attractive to new clients. Often, all it takes is an inflated number in the final contract year, which the team will most likely never pay, to catapult the average salary into the top tier of the position group on paper. Meanwhile, this has nothing to do with the contract's actual impact on the team's further roster planning.

Far more important are metrics such as guaranteed payments, cap hits, dead cap, cash flow up to the earliest exit scenario and how the cap charges are distributed over the life of the contract. Especially with high-priced quarterback contracts, which often take up more than 20 percent of the salary cap, it becomes clear how important a thorough understanding of the contract structure is.

### Why APY/AAV are not meaningful and what really matters

APY or AAV merely reflect a player's average annual earnings based on the contract years and the published maximum value of the contract, and thus suggest stability or comparability between contracts. But these values ignore fundamental aspects such as:

- When payments are due.
- How much is actually guaranteed.
- How the contract affects the salary cap.

Put simply in business terms, "APY" is like a superficial look at a company's revenue: it says nothing about the cost structure, the profit margins or long-term liquidity.

To get a better understanding of the parameters that really matter in an assessment, here is a short explanation of the key aspects:

### Base salary vs. signing bonus

How compensation is split between base salaries and signing bonuses has a direct impact on a team's salary cap charges. Base salaries count fully against the salary cap (the annual spending limit) in the year they are paid. This can mean a higher financial burden in the short term but offers flexibility for later adjustments, since parts of the base salary can be converted into a signing bonus.

A signing bonus, in contrast, is often paid out in full when the contract is signed but spread over several years on the salary cap (five years at most). It is therefore similar to depreciation in accounting, for example when the cost of a car is spread over its useful life.

This practice allows teams to reduce today's cap charge despite a large payment to the player and to free up resources under the salary cap for other players. Teams that use large signing bonuses therefore create room to maneuver today but accept higher obligations in the long run.

### The advantage of higher cap hits in later contract years

A frequently used concept is shifting cap hits into the later years of a contract. This strategy makes particular sense when the NFL salary cap keeps rising, as it has in recent years. Because the NFL is growing economically through new TV deals and rising revenues, a high cap hit in the future will be less of a burden relative to a higher salary cap than it is today. As an example, take a contract that guarantees a player the same amount every year for five years. Say $50 million, with the salary cap rising from $255 million to more than $330 million in 2028, according to projections by Overthecap.com.

| Year | 2024 | 2025 | 2026 | 2027 | 2028 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Salary cap in $M | 255.40 | 272.50 | 290.00 | 314.00 | 331.30 |
| Salary in $M | 50.00 | 50.00 | 50.00 | 50.00 | 50.00 |
| Share of cap | 19.6% | 18.3% | 17.2% | 15.9% | 15.1% |
| Salary at 2024 share in $M | 50.00 | 53.35 | 56.77 | 61.47 | 64.86 |
| Notional savings in $M | 0.00 | 3.35 | 6.77 | 11.47 | 14.86 |

As you can see, thanks to the long contract term the team "saves" almost $15 million in 2028 compared with simply offering the player one-year deals at the same percentage of the salary cap. The roster planners then use these notional savings for other players.

This approach allows teams to invest more in other key positions now in order to be competitive right away. It is comparable to a business strategy in which a company makes investments today with borrowed capital that only has to be fully repaid in the future. As long as revenues rise as projected, this practice is sustainable in the long run.

### The role of restructures

Restructures are an essential tool for creating cap space in the short term. Part of the base salary is converted into a signing bonus, which reduces this year's cap charge and spreads it over the remaining contract years. This option is particularly valuable for reacting to unexpected challenges, for example when signing a free agent or dealing with injuries.

A contract with a high base salary offers more room for such adjustments, whereas a contract built heavily on signing bonuses is less flexible. Teams should be careful, though, since restructuring too often can lead to cap charges piling up in later years, which jeopardizes financial flexibility in the long run.

### How do guarantees play out?

Guarantees are the central factor in NFL contracts because they fix a team's financial obligations regardless of the player's future. High guarantees mean security for the player but increase the risk for the team, especially if the player's performance declines or injuries occur.

Another element that affects guarantees is dead cap. It arises when a player is released before all signing bonuses or guaranteed salaries have been fully charged against the salary cap. To create short-term cap relief, teams often use so-called void years: artificially added contract years that allow bonuses to be spread over a longer period. However, this practice increases dead cap costs in the future, when the player's contract ends or he is released. The dead cap then immediately reduces the salary cap.

### Examples from recent years

Based on the parameters just explained, two contracts can be compared well using the figures that have become public (sources: overthecap.com and spotrac.com):

![Comparison of example contracts](https://i0.wp.com/theninerempiregermany.de/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/BeispielVertraege.png?resize=723%2C340&ssl=1)

### Jalen Hurts: focus on bonuses and low base salaries (2023)

Jalen Hurts' contract is heavily geared toward signing bonuses and low base salaries in the first years. This structure offers two main advantages:

- **Short-term cap relief:** Signing bonuses can be spread over several years, which drastically reduces the cap hits in the first years of the contract. Hurts' cap hit in 2023 was only $6.15 million and in 2024 about $13.56 million, a fraction of what he actually earns. This allows the Eagles to invest in key areas such as the offensive line or the defense during Hurts' prime.
- **Predictable burden in later years:** The big cap hits only come in later contract years, when the NFL salary cap will likely be significantly higher thanks to rising revenue from TV deals and other sources. The relative burden is therefore smaller, even though the nominal numbers are high.

Strategic advantage:

The structure resembles a "start-up approach" in business, where resources are freed up today for short-term investments in order to secure long-term success. The Eagles can build a competitive team around Hurts today without losing immediate financial flexibility.

Risks:

If, contrary to expectations, the salary cap does not rise as projected or Hurts' performance declines, the high cap hits in later years (up to $54 million) could become a problem, as could the dead cap that might result from an early release.

### Patrick Mahomes: higher base salaries with long-term flexibility (2020)

Patrick Mahomes' contract runs for ten years and, compared with Hurts' contract, contains relatively high base salaries that can, however, be restructured flexibly. This structure also offers clear advantages:

- **Long-term stability:** Mahomes' contract ties him to the Kansas City Chiefs for the long term. This gives the team planning security over a longer period without having to constantly negotiate new contracts.
- **Flexibility through restructures:** Mahomes' contract allows the Chiefs to convert base salaries into signing bonuses through restructures. This lets them reduce cap hits in problematic years and push them into later years. In recent years, the Chiefs have regularly adjusted Mahomes' cap hits to free up money for other commitments.
- **No sudden cap spikes:** The contract does not contain extremely low cap hits at the start but spreads the burden relatively evenly over the years. As a result, there are no years with suddenly exploding cap hits that could restrict the team's room to maneuver.

Strategic advantage:

Mahomes' contract resembles a "diversified investment" in business: the Chiefs spread the burden more evenly while keeping the option of reacting to new situations through restructures.

Risks:

The long-term nature of the contract carries a certain risk: if Mahomes were seriously injured or his performance dropped drastically, the contract could become a financial burden in the long run. However, this risk is relatively small thanks to the option of restructuring.

### Jordan Love: short-term extension with immediate payout and an option for more (2022)

In Jordan Love's case, it is worth mentioning that this was already his second extension with the Packers. Love's third rookie year ended in 2023, and the Packers had to decide whether to exercise the fifth-year option for first-round picks. But since Love had only been Aaron Rodgers' backup up to that point and the Packers did not yet know whether Love was the right long-term QB, they gave Love a one-year extension of his rookie contract instead of the fifth-year option. The Packers wanted more time to evaluate Jordan Love as a long-term starter before paying the expensive fifth-year option or signing a costly multi-year deal. Had Green Bay exercised Love's fifth-year option, it would have cost them $20.3 million, fully guaranteed. The new contract reduced the guaranteed amount to $13.5 million, while Love could still get close to that figure through performance-based incentives.

For the Packers, this meant savings of about $6.8 million unless Love hit all of his incentives. And had Love disappointed in the 2023 season, the Packers would have been able to get out of the contract more cheaply than if they had had to pay the fifth-year option. In addition, Love received a significant raise for the 2023 season compared with his rookie contract.

### Summary

These contracts show quite clearly how differently teams can approach their quarterbacks' contracts. If you compare the APY figure announced to the media with the cap charges actually incurred so far, you see a clear difference. Patrick Mahomes' 2020 contract was promoted with an APY of $45 million, but so far it has only led to average cap charges of $24.2 million per year. However, a cut in the upcoming offseason would mean dead cap of $77 million. Jalen Hurts' contract was announced in 2023 with an APY of $51 million but has so far only been on the books with a cap hit of just under $10 million per year. The cap hit does not rise above $41 million until 2027. A release in the coming offseason would result in dead cap of $107 million.

It is also interesting how high, non-guaranteed base salaries, especially in the final contract years, are used to climb the APY table and thus present a better picture of the agent in the media. Tua Tagovailoa, for example, has $41.4 million in the final year of his contract, a relatively odd number compared with the previous years. The reason is most likely that those extra $400,000 bring Tua to an APY of $53.1 million, surpassing Jared Goff's contract by $100,000 in APY. That makes the agent look better.

### How does the price of the QB affect a team's chances of success?

How much of the salary cap goes to the quarterback (QB) position varies considerably among NFL teams, especially among playoff teams. An analysis of recent seasons by Jason Fitzgerald of Overthecap.com shows that successful teams no longer on a rookie contract frequently spend a moderate to high share of their salary cap on their QBs.

### Distribution of salary cap shares ([according to OvertheCap](https://overthecap.com/qb-salary-cap-charges-and-the-playoffs)):

- **11 to 13 percent of the salary cap:** This range has the highest success rate, with 59.1 percent of teams reaching the playoffs. With a salary cap of $272 million (2025 projection), this corresponds to a cap hit between $29 million and $36 million.
- **13 to 15 percent of the salary cap:** Here 50 percent of teams reach the playoffs, which corresponds to a cap hit of $36 million to $41 million.
- **15 to 17 percent of the salary cap:** In this segment, 55.6 percent of teams make the playoffs, with QB cap hits between $41 million and $47 million.

It is notable that teams with a very high QB salary (more than 17 percent of the salary cap) have a lower success rate of only 20 percent. This suggests that an excessively high share of the salary cap for a single player can hurt the depth and flexibility of the entire roster.

Teams that spend between 11 and 17 percent of their salary cap on the QB position (after a restructure, if necessary) tend to have better chances of reaching the playoffs. A balanced relationship between paying the quarterback and keeping financial flexibility for other positions appears to be crucial for team success.

### So what now? What will the 49ers do with Brock Purdy?

In light of all this, it is clear that Brock Purdy's extension is about much more than the APY values that the current debate revolves around. Some demand at least $60 million APY for him, others won't even grant him $40 million. Other German podcasters even argue that the extension should be postponed and only negotiated at the end of next season, when the franchise tag also becomes an option.

> "Franchise tag x2 is what I would do. Alternatively an extension you can get out of after 2 years." (translated from German)
>
> Adrian Franke (@adrianbb89), [December 13, 2024](https://twitter.com/adrianbb89/status/1867510265778208774)

In any case, one can already say that unless Purdy collapses in the manner of Daniel Jones, the 49ers still have a chance at a successful season no matter what contract they give him. The QB contract alone says nothing about whether a team can be competitive or not. The many different contracts show that clearly.

## Possible scenarios for Brock Purdy

### Prove-it deal (Jordan Love, 2023)

In this scenario, which Mike Sando of The Athletic once hinted at, the 49ers follow the Packers' path: they are not really sure whether Purdy is the long-term starter but want to reward him appropriately for his performances, and they postpone the final decision by one year with at least a bearable cap hit. In that case, the 49ers could offer him a slightly increased guaranteed salary for the 2025 season as part of a two-year deal (effectively an early one-year extension through 2026) while paying out a large signing bonus spread over the two contract years and several void years. To protect Purdy, they could grant him another deferred (prorated) bonus for 2026 that becomes guaranteed at a certain date (e.g. April 1, 2026). Such a deal could be a win-win scenario. Right after signing, Purdy gets the money he would have received as the first overall pick, including a 2026 fifth-year option in the form of the conditional bonus. The 49ers get one more year to make a final decision, and if the season doesn't go well, they can end the relationship at bearable cost after the season. Here is an example calculation using Overthecap.com's Contract Constructor:

> This would mean Top5 APY contract and big cashout for Purdy (more than he would have made as Top3 Pick), so he gets rewarded for his rookie years and after 2025 its either kind of 5th year option, new contract or affordable dead money for 49ers…
>
> Chris Pracher (@CPracher497), [December 5, 2024](https://twitter.com/CPracher497/status/1864711077725929579)

### Mid-term deal with high staggered bonuses (Jalen Hurts, 2023)

Jalen Hurts' contract has already been explained in detail. Such a contract would keep Purdy's cap charge to a minimum in the first contract years (2025 to 2027) while already giving him large cash payouts. Thanks to the low cap charge, the 49ers could continue to pay other players well, for example sign free agents or extend their own players. With such a structure, an APY of more than $60 million could be reached, for instance, which would certainly please the agent, while the 49ers would initially only carry a cap charge of $10 million to $35 million. Depending on how the bonus payments are triggered in the following years, an early exit could also be absorbed, as the resulting dead cap would weigh less heavily thanks to the increased salary cap than it appears today.

### The long-term deal with plenty of room to maneuver (Patrick Mahomes, 2020)

If Shanahan, Lynch and York are sure that Purdy is the QB who should start for the 49ers for the next seven to eight years, a long-term structure like the ones the Chiefs used for Mahomes or the Bills for Josh Allen would also be an option. In terms of APY, however, no record deal should be expected, since the payments are stretched over a much longer period and the value for Purdy and his agent lies more in the total value of the contract, which might then be around $250 million to $300 million over five to seven years (ESPN's Bill Barnwell even speculates about $325 million). In terms of salary cap charges, however, the 49ers would keep full room to maneuver. A deal could, for example, include a large signing bonus in exchange for low base salaries in the first two years. From year three, the base salary would rise but would then offer the option of using a restructure to take advantage of the rising salary cap and lower the percentage burden. This long-term deal would give Purdy and the 49ers certainty about a lasting partnership. However, a drop in performance or a serious injury would be very hard for the 49ers to absorb, depending on the agreed guarantees. Deshaun Watson is probably the best cautionary example of that.

### A best-of from all contracts (Trevor Lawrence)

Since Purdy's agent also represents Trevor Lawrence, it seems obvious that the answer here might lie in a combined solution. After his extension, Lawrence's contract still runs for seven years in total, so five new years were added, bringing it close to Mahomes. Only after five years does the base salary rise above $50 million; before that it is at most $11 million. So at the start of the contract a structure like Jalen Hurts' was chosen, while the later high but non-guaranteed base salaries leave room for restructures:

![Trevor Lawrence contract](https://i0.wp.com/theninerempiregermany.de/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/LawrenceVertrag.png?resize=712%2C406&ssl=1)

## Summary and conclusion

Brock Purdy's upcoming contract extension gives the San Francisco 49ers the opportunity to make a strategically smart decision, and fans should keep one important lesson in mind: the often-quoted "average per year" (APY) is not a meaningful yardstick for evaluating quarterback contracts. APY ignores crucial details made possible by the CBA, such as the actual cap charge in each year, the distribution of guaranteed money and the flexibility a contract offers through restructures. What matters much more is how a contract is built: contracts that combine large signing bonuses with low initial cap hits, as with Jalen Hurts, allow maximum investment in the rest of the roster. At the same time, later cap hits should be considered in light of a growing salary cap in order to spread the burden for the team, an approach that is especially evident in Mahomes' contract. Whether the 49ers choose a cautious, performance-based solution as with Jordan Love, a mid-term structure as with Jalen Hurts or a long-term model as with Patrick Mahomes depends on how strongly they see Purdy as their franchise quarterback of the future. The key is to find a balance that reflects Purdy's value and also positions the team for sustained success in the years ahead. One thing you can be sure of, though: the QB contract alone says nothing about whether the team can be successful in the future. Many more factors come into play there. But that is another, even longer story.

Finally, I hope this year-end piece was able to answer some questions and contribute to a deeper understanding of this complex topic.

With that in mind: Go Niners!

*(All figures and details are based on reports from Overthecap.com, Spotrac, ProFootballTalk and ESPN. Figures may differ in places, since contract details are not officially published.)*
